UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                      )
                                                      )
                  MISO Legacy Queue                   )                 Docket No. ER26-3813-000
                  Acceleration Proposal               )
                                                      )


                         COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED



         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Advanced Energy United (“United”) 2 submits these comments

in support of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s (“MISO”) September 21, 2026,

submission of revisions to MISO’s Attachment X, Generator Interconnection Procedures

(“GIP”), of its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff

(“Tariff”).3 The revisions give MISO “sufficient tools to clear” DPP-2022, its last legacy queue

cycle, and prevent unlimited restudies in Phase III of the Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”). 4

United supports the proposed Legacy Queue Acceleration Framework as a targeted measure to

help MISO reduce its interconnection backlog and provide greater certainty for projects that have

remained in the queue for an extended period. MISO’s proposal is consistent with Orders No.




1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure, clean
and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents the full
range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy includes
energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and more. The
comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not represent the views
of any particular member with respect to any issue.
3
  Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Legacy Queue Acceleration Proposal and Request for Expedited Action,
Shortened Comment Period, and Waiver of the Sixty-Day Prior Notice Requirement, Docket No. ER26-3813
(September 21, 2026). (“Transmittal Letter”)
4
  Transmittal, at 1.


                                                                                                                   1
 2003 and 2023,5 and effectively addresses the concerns around legacy withdrawals given the

current late stage of DPP-2022. United requests the Commission approve the legacy queue

revisions as just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.6

    I.      Background

         MISO’s interconnection queue remains severely backlogged. A recent progress report

produced for Advanced Energy United by The Brattle Group and Grid Strategies described

MISO as having “incomplete progress,” while most other regions were described as having

“promising improvements” or “expected progress.”7 The report noted the significant backlog and

cascading delays as particular concerns in the MISO region. 8

         DPP-2022 presents particular timing and certainty concerns because it is MISO’s largest

queue cycle to date, beginning with 911 interconnection requests totaling approximately 161.2

GW of proposed generation capacity.9 As a result of ongoing queue backlogs, MISO has

introduced and proposed alternative interconnection pathways to address Resource Adequacy

needs, specifically, the Expedited Resource Addition Study process, and the forthcoming Large

Load Addition Resource Study. To date, MISO has done very little to tackle DPP queue

backlogs. MISO explains that, absent targeted tariff revisions, late-stage withdrawals in DPP-

2022 could trigger cascading restudies, shifting cost allocations, and additional delays for

projects that remain in the queue.


5

61,287 (2004), order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff'd sub nom. Nat'l Ass'n of Regul.
Util. Comm'rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007); Improvements to Generator Interconnection Procedures &
Agreements, Order No. 2023, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054 (2023), order on reh'g, Order No. 2023-A, 186 FERC ¶ 61,199
(2024). (“Order 2023”; “Order 2003”)
6
  16 U.S.C. § 824d(a), (a).
7
  Generator Interconnection Interim Progress Report, Advanced Energy United, at 4 (June 2026).
https://advancedenergyunited.org/reports/interconnection-progress-report/
8
  Id., at 26-27.
9
  Transmittal, at 6.


                                                                                                              2
            Under MISO’s existing tariff, Phase III restudies may continue without a defined

endpoint when withdrawals or other changes require additional analysis. MISO states that this

framework could undermine the cost certainty and finality interconnection customers need to

make informed commercial decisions, particularly at this late stage of DPP-2022.10 To address

these concerns, MISO proposes three targeted reforms: a one-time penalty-free withdrawal

opportunity for DPP-2022 customers before Decision Point II closes; an increased withdrawal-

penalty threshold for customers that remain in DPP-2022 after Decision Point II; and a limit of

one final Phase III restudy for DPP-2022 and future queue cycles.11 MISO developed the

proposal through stakeholder discussions on an expedited timeline and requests Commission

action by October 19, 2026, so that the penalty-free withdrawal opportunity is available before

Decision Point II closes.12

           MISO’s proposal is intended to give interconnection customers a limited opportunity to

exit the queue, reduce the risk of repeated Phase III restudies, and provide greater certainty for

DPP-2022 and future queue cycles.

     II.      Comments

           Given the severe backlog in MISO’s interconnection process and the halting progress to

date in processing years-old interconnection requests, it is clear that bold action is needed if the

region is going to achieve its target of a one-year interconnection cycle and return to reliance on

the standard interconnection process as the pathway for fair and efficient resource entry. It is in

this context that United supports MISO’s proposed Legacy Queue Acceleration Framework as a

targeted response to repeated cycle disruptions in DPP-2022. The proposal also advances the



10
   Transmittal, at 2.
11
   Id., at 10-12.
12
   Id., at 9-10.


                                                                                                       3
 Commission’s goal of an interconnection process that is efficient, timely, and sufficiently certain

to support commercial decisions. Unbounded restudies undermine those interconnection goals;

each withdrawal can alter the network upgrade cost assignments on which remaining customers

rely to finance, contract, and build their projects. By pairing a one-time, penalty-free withdrawal

opportunity before Decision Point II with limits on later restudies, 13 MISO’s proposal encourages

timely exits, helps establish a more realistic set of projects entering Phase III, and provides

greater certainty for projects that remain in the queue. While MISO’s limitation on restudies for

DPP-2022 and all subsequent clusters comes with clear tradeoffs, the potential adverse effects of

this change can be minimized if MISO commits to ensure that, in the absence of a full restudy, it

conducts a screening to eliminate network upgrades rendered unnecessary as a result of project

withdrawals. Accordingly, the Commission should approve the proposal as a just and reasonable

means of restoring certainty to DPP-2022 and future queue cycles.

                     A. Expedited Commission approval ahead of MISO’s requested effective
                        date is critical to the success of the proposal.

            The practical value of MISO’s proposal depends on Commission action before the

Decision Point II window closes. The proposed penalty-free withdrawal opportunity is designed

to give DPP-2022 customers a clear and timely choice: either exit the queue before Phase III

begins or remain in the cycle with a more stable project set. That opportunity will be meaningful

only if customers know that the Commission has accepted the tariff revisions before the Decision

Point II deadline, when interconnection customers will have to make withdrawal decisions.

            Decision Point II for DPP-2022 is scheduled to close on October 20, 2026.14 Commission

action after the scheduled close will substantially diminish the central benefit of the proposal, as


13
     Transmittal, at 8.
14
     Id., at 13.


                                                                                                       4
 it would force interconnection customers to make their Decision Point II elections without

certainty as to whether the penalty-free withdrawal option will apply. This would result in Phase

III commencing with the same uncertainty and potential instability that MISO’s filing seeks to

address.

        The window is useful only if customers can make informed decisions. When customers

decide whether to stay or withdraw, they should know their current cost exposure and how

withdrawals from the cycle could shift costs among the remaining projects. Expedited approval

would allow customers to make informed decisions, reduce the likelihood of unnecessary Phase

III restudies, and help ensure that Phase III begins with a more stable and realistic set of projects.

       It is therefore imperative for the Commission to expedite action, per MISO’s request. It is

equally imperative for MISO to give DPP-2022 customers, before Decision Point II concludes,

the most current cost and allocation information available and a clear statement of what it does

and does not reflect. This will provide customers with the best opportunity to make informed

withdrawal decisions, and MISO can do this within its existing study schedule and without

changing the filing. In the absence of Commission action before Decision Point II closes, MISO

should promptly solicit information from DPP-2022 customers regarding whether they would

have withdrawn had the penalty-free withdrawal option been in effect. Doing so would preserve

MISO’s ability to apply the option retroactively if the Commission subsequently accepts the

proposal.

               B. Allowing only a single Phase III restudy is a reasonable measure to ensure
                  timely completion of DPP-2022, but comes with tradeoffs that should be
                  mitigated to the extent possible.

       MISO’s proposed Phase III restudy limit effectively addresses the uncertainty of potential

late-stage withdrawals that will trigger repeated restudies; these restudies could shift network




                                                                                                     5
 upgrade cost allocations and delay final results for customers that remain in the queue. MISO’s

proposed revisions would permit only one Phase III restudy, and only where necessary to ensure

the reliability of the Transmission System. 15 If a restudy is needed, customers will be informed

and given five days to proceed or withdrawal; if no restudy is needed, MISO would rely on prior

study results and reallocate costs among the remaining interconnection customers. 16 This

approach is a reasonable means of balancing reliability needs against the need for finality, cost

certainty, and timely queue administration.

         The single-restudy limit is particularly important for DPP-2022, where customers are

already making commercial decisions at a late stage in a large and complex queue cycle. Under

the existing framework, each withdrawal can create the possibility of another restudy, which can

in turn change cost assignments and extend the timeline for customers that have continued to

invest in their projects.17 By establishing a defined endpoint for Phase III restudies, MISO’s

proposal gives remaining customers a more stable basis for financing, contracting, procurement,

and other project-development decisions. That certainty is also consistent with the Commission’s

broader interconnection reforms.

         While United supports the proposed one-restudy limitation as a reasonable means of

advancing queue finality and completing DPP-2022, limiting restudies necessarily involves

tradeoffs that must be considered. A limitation on Phase III restudies may create circumstances

where network upgrades identified prior to significant project withdrawals are assigned to

remaining customers even if those upgrades would no longer be required under a fully restudied

cluster. MISO provides only limited safeguards against this outcome, namely a conditional



15
   Transmittal, at 10-11.
16
   Id., at 12.
17
   Id., at 3.


                                                                                                    6
 restudy when deemed necessary to ensure reliability and the potential for cost reallocation

without restudies.18 This tradeoff is reasonable given the proposal’s certainty and queue

processing efficiency benefits; however, where practicable and without conducting an additional

full Phase III restudy, MISO should conduct a targeted review to determine whether previously

identified network upgrades are still needed after significant withdrawals, allowing MISO to

remove any unnecessary upgrades from final cost allocation.

           United does not ask the Commission to reject or condition MISO’s proposal on that basis

because the cost and timing uncertainty created by repeated restudies is itself a serious problem,

and MISO’s proposal reasonably prioritizes establishing finality while preserving the ability to

conduct one reliability-driven restudy where necessary. At the same time, the Commission

should encourage MISO to provide transparency, including future BPM language, around

implementation of the single-restudy limit. It is crucial that interconnection customers receive

clarity around steps MISO will take to avoid assignment of network upgrades rendered

unnecessary by project withdrawals in the absence of a full restudy. If MISO determines that a

restudy is necessary to ensure reliability, affected customers should receive a written explanation

identifying the reliability basis for that determination and the facilities or constraints involved.

Customers also should receive updated cost and cost allocation information at the same time as

any restudy notice, so that they can make an informed decision within the proposed five-

business-day election window. A short decision window may be reasonable if it supports

schedule certainty, but it is only workable if customers have the information needed to evaluate

the consequences of proceeding or withdrawing.




18
     Transmittal, at 11-12.


                                                                                                       7
             The Commission should also clarify the limited application of the proposed withdrawal

consequences following a restudy election. Under MISO’s proposal, a customer that elects to

proceed with a restudy and later withdraws would be treated as a post-GIA withdrawal.19 The

provision appears designed to prevent a customer who chooses to continue after a restudy notice

from imposing additional disruption on the remaining queue at low cost. But because that

consequence is significant, the Commission should confirm that it applies only to customers that

affirmatively elect to proceed after receiving a restudy notice, and not to withdrawals occurring

in other circumstances.

            With these clarifications, the single-restudy limit can preserve MISO’s ability to conduct

a reliability-driven restudy while giving customers a clear endpoint and more stable costs.

                     C. The higher penalty-free withdrawal threshold after Decision Point II is a
                        reasonable trade-off to enhance certainty for remaining cluster
                        participants.

            MISO’s proposed higher threshold for penalty-free withdrawal after Decision Point II is a

reasonable exchange for the one-time exit opportunity. Customers that stay in the queue face a

higher bar for penalty-free withdrawal relative to the 35% network upgrade cost increase that

applies today. Specifically, under MISO’s proposal, interconnection customers are only allowed a

penalty free withdrawal if they face a network upgrade cost increase of more than 50%, together

with an increase of at least $15,000 per MW from the revised System Impact Study to the Final

System Impact Study.20 This higher threshold comes with a tradeoff in that it increases the risk of

a withdrawal penalty even after a significant cost increase, but in exchange it ensures that

customers that stay after the withdrawal period have accepted the project’s viability and cost


19
     Transmittal, at 12.
20
     Id., at 10.



                                                                                                         8
 exposure. Additionally, by requiring customers to bear more cost variability before they can

withdraw without penalty, the higher threshold supports the certainty the proposal is meant to

create for the remaining projects. The proposed DPP-2022 exit window is also unconditional and

gives customers the chance to leave before the higher threshold applies. The proposal’s

reasonableness is reinforced by this structure: customers receive a narrow, one-time opportunity

to exit before Decision Point II, but those that remain are subject to a higher threshold for

penalty-free withdrawal going forward. This is not a general loosening of the withdrawal rules.

                     D. The proposal sufficiently satisfies the independent entity variation
                        standard as it is narrowly tailored and consistent with the Commission’s
                        goals to improve interconnection.

           MISO’s proposal constitutes an independent entity variation as it does not follow the pro

forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures.21 The proposal satisfies the Commission’s

independent entity variation standard because it is of limited scope, transparently administered,

and directly responsive to unique circumstances affecting interconnection. The Commission has

long recognized the need for region-specific variations when the variations are supported by

operational realities and are just and reasonable. In the present circumstances, MISO has

demonstrated extraordinary circumstances posing undue risk to DPP-2022 absent intervention.

DPP-2022, the largest legacy cluster, has experienced repeated delays and remains vulnerable to

cascading withdrawals and restudies that threaten to further postpone final study results.22

MISO’s proposal reasonably alleviates these threats by narrowly focusing on specific withdrawal

challenges, rather than creating a broad change to the interconnection framework.




21
     Transmittal, at 12-13.
22
     Id., at 2.


                                                                                                       9
         The penalty-free withdrawal window is sufficiently limited in scope to not constitute a

risk to the greater interconnection framework. The withdrawal window is limited to a single

cycle and defined decision point, preventing broad application that would disrupt further cycles.

The withdrawal is also available to all customers; MISO has no discretion over which customers

can withdrawal from DPP-2022 before the conclusion of Decision Point II. 23 Similarly, the

increased withdrawal threshold applies only to customers that voluntarily elect to remain in the

cluster after the withdrawal window closes. The restudy limit applies uniformly to all future

cycles and does not provide preferential treatment to any particular customer or customer

classes.24 These features demonstrate the proposals careful tailoring to address identified

problems while easing potential concerns about undue discrimination.

        Further, the proposed revisions are consistent with, and advance, the Commission’s

broader efforts to improve generator interconnection. Through multiple interconnection focused

orders, the Commission has emphasized the importance of reducing interconnection delays,

increasing certainty, and ensuring timely and efficient request processing;25 all of which align

with MISO’s revisions. Unlimited or repeated restudies would undermine the Commission’s

goals by extending study timelines and introducing uncertainty regarding network upgrade costs

and project viability. If paired with a targeted review to determine whether previously identified

network upgrades are still needed after significant withdrawals, as recommended above, the

proposed restudy limit will provide increased speed and certainty without risk of inefficient

outcomes. By creating a mechanism for customers to make informed withdrawal decisions


23
   Transmittal, at 9.
24
   Id., at 10.
25
   Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements & Proc., Order No. 2003, 104 F.E.R.C. ¶ 61,103, P 11-
14 (2003); Improvements to Generator Interconnection Proc. & Agreements, Order No. 2023, 184 F.E.R.C. ¶
61,054, P 1, 27-34 (2023).




                                                                                                              10
 before Phase III and by establishing a defined endpoint for restudy activity, MISO’s proposal

promotes the cost certainty, efficiency, and queue finality that the Commission has repeatedly

identified as essential components of a functional interconnection process.

       Overall, MISO’s proposal is a sufficiently targeted response to the legacy backlog that, if

successful at accelerating DPP-2022 and subsequent clusters, will create a foundation upon

which to consider further reforms. While a positive development, the proposal should not be read

as a substitute for more foundational reform of MISO’s standard interconnection process. MISO

should continue to develop improvements that deliver timely, predictable, and equitable access to

the transmission system for all customers, including those in future cycles. Although the single-

restudy limit represents a meaningful step toward addressing the challenges posed by legacy

queue backlogs and withdrawal-driven restudies, additional reforms may be needed to ensure a

timely, predictable, and equitable interconnection process longer term. United encourages MISO

to build on the momentum this proposal presents to undertake more foundational, lasting

interconnection reforms that deliver greater upfront cost certainty to address the root cause of

withdrawals and cascading restudies that precipitated the need for this proposal in the first place.

               E. Conclusion

       For the reasons stated above, Advanced Energy United respectfully requests that the

Commission consider these comments and accept MISO’s proposed Legacy Queue Acceleration.




       Respectfully submitted,
